title: Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment: Function, Cognition, Medications, Supports, and Goals
bottomLine: Comprehensive geriatric assessment is multidomain and goal-driven: medical conditions alone do not explain function. Assess cognition, mood, mobility/falls, medications, continence, nutrition, sensory function, ADLs/IADLs, social supports, caregiver burden and goals, then prioritize the problems most likely to improve safety and quality of life.
recognize: New dependence may reflect reversible illness, medication burden, delirium, depression, sensory loss or environmental barriers rather than irreversible aging.
Caregiver strain and access barriers can determine whether a medical plan is feasible.
differentiate: Frailty, disability and multimorbidity overlap but are not synonyms.
Screening tools support assessment but do not replace patient/caregiver history and observed function.
assessment: Review ADLs/IADLs, gait/falls, cognition, mood, hearing/vision, nutrition/weight, continence, medication list, pain, sleep, living situation, supports, finances/access and goals of care.
workup: Use targeted testing for reversible contributors and validated cognitive/frailty/fall tools when they change management; avoid indiscriminate panels.
management: Create a prioritized interprofessional plan that reduces treatment burden, improves mobility/safety and aligns disease targets with goals/life expectancy.
medicationSafety: Perform medication reconciliation and identify anticholinergic/sedative/hypotensive burden and prescribing cascades.
redFlags: Unsafe living situation or caregiver collapse
counselling: Ask what matters most and explain tradeoffs among longevity, function, symptom relief and treatment burden.
followUp: Track function and implementation of referrals/medication changes, not only disease metrics.
examTrap: Applying disease-specific targets independently until the combined regimen worsens falls, cognition and quality of life.
oneLinePearl: Geriatric assessment asks what the person can do, what matters, and what the treatment is costing them.
sourceBasis: Canadian geriatric medicine and comprehensive geriatric assessment practice principles

title: Falls Risk Assessment and Prevention: Find the Modifiable Contributors
bottomLine: A fall is a syndrome, not a diagnosis. Determine whether it was mechanical, syncopal, medication-related, neurologic, cardiovascular or environmental, then address gait/strength, orthostasis, vision, footwear/home hazards and medication burden rather than prescribing generic 'fall precautions'.
recognize: Prior falls, gait/balance impairment, sedatives, orthostatic hypotension, vision loss and muscle weakness are major risk signals.
Injury may be occult in osteoporosis, anticoagulation or cognitive impairment.
differentiate: Syncope or seizure is not a simple trip; unexplained falls may be the presenting symptom.
Fear of falling can reduce activity and worsen deconditioning, creating a cycle.
assessment: Reconstruct the event, assess orthostatic vitals, gait/balance, footwear, vision/hearing, neurologic/cardiac findings, medications, alcohol, osteoporosis and home context.
workup: Use ECG/labs/imaging only when the history/exam suggests syncope, injury or medical cause; avoid routine head imaging for every uncomplicated fall.
management: Use strength/balance exercise or PT, home hazard modification, vision/footwear correction, medication optimization and osteoporosis/fracture prevention as indicated.
medicationSafety: Review benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, anticholinergics, opioids and excessive BP-lowering; taper rather than abruptly stop dependence-forming agents.
redFlags: Hip fracture inability to bear weight
counselling: Frame prevention around maintaining mobility and independence rather than restricting activity.
followUp: Track recurrent falls, gait and completion of PT/home/medication interventions.
examTrap: Telling an older adult to 'be more careful' without checking orthostasis and a new sedative prescription.
oneLinePearl: Falls prevention is contributor reduction plus strength—not caution alone.

title: Frailty Recognition and Management: Vulnerability Is More Than Age
bottomLine: Frailty is reduced physiologic reserve and vulnerability to stressors, not simply older age or multiple diagnoses. Identify it to adjust treatment intensity, prevent deconditioning, plan transitions and clarify goals—without using a frailty label to deny beneficial care automatically.
recognize: Weight loss, weakness, slowness, exhaustion, low activity and accumulation of deficits can signal frailty.
Small acute stressors can cause disproportionate functional decline in frail adults.
differentiate: Frailty differs from disability, dementia and terminal illness though they may coexist.
Acute illness can transiently worsen frailty measures and should not be mistaken for a fixed baseline.
assessment: Assess baseline function, mobility, weight/nutrition, cognition, comorbidity, medications, social supports, goals and recovery after recent stressors.
workup: Use a validated frailty measure appropriate to setting and investigate reversible contributors such as anemia, depression, malnutrition or medication toxicity.
management: Prioritize resistance/physical activity, nutrition, medication simplification, vaccination, fall prevention and proactive care planning; tailor invasive/procedural decisions to risks, benefits and goals rather than age alone.
medicationSafety: Lower physiologic reserve increases adverse drug effects; start/titrate cautiously where appropriate and deprescribe low-benefit therapy.
redFlags: Inability to recover after minor illness
counselling: Explain frailty as potentially modifiable vulnerability and avoid fatalistic language.
followUp: Track function and recovery, not only disease numbers.
examTrap: Using chronological age as a proxy for frailty or using frailty to deny a treatment without individualized benefit-risk assessment.
oneLinePearl: Frailty measures reserve; age measures time.

title: Polypharmacy and Deprescribing: Every Drug Needs a Current Job
bottomLine: Polypharmacy is harmful when medication burden exceeds benefit, not simply when the pill count is high. Reconcile all prescriptions/OTC/supplements, identify indication, benefit horizon, duplication, interactions and adverse effects, then deprescribe collaboratively with tapering/monitoring where withdrawal or rebound is possible.
recognize: Falls, confusion, constipation, urinary retention, orthostasis and appetite decline can be medication effects or prescribing cascades.
Preventive drugs may have a time-to-benefit that no longer matches goals or life expectancy.
differentiate: Appropriate multimorbidity treatment can require many medications; the target is inappropriate burden, not an arbitrary number.
Stopping a drug is an active therapeutic intervention requiring monitoring.
assessment: Build a best possible medication history including OTC/herbals, adherence, indications, perceived benefit, adverse effects and patient priorities.
workup: Use labs/monitoring required for specific drugs and assess renal/hepatic function; avoid adding another drug before considering whether a current medication caused the symptom.
management: Prioritize high-risk/low-benefit medications, stop duplicates, simplify regimens and taper dependence/rebound-prone agents with shared decision-making.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, anticholinergics, opioids and hypoglycemia-causing drugs require particular risk review but are not stopped abruptly without context.
counselling: Explain what is being stopped, why, what to expect and what symptoms would trigger reassessment.
followUp: Review symptoms and function after each meaningful deprescribing step and update all medication lists.
examTrap: Adding an anticholinergic for incontinence caused by a medication cascade without reviewing the original regimen.
oneLinePearl: Deprescribing is prescribing in reverse: indication, plan, taper, monitor.

title: Dementia in Older Adults: Diagnose Decline, Preserve Autonomy, Support Caregivers
bottomLine: Dementia is acquired cognitive decline that interferes with independent function and is not an inevitable part of aging. Establish baseline and trajectory, exclude delirium/depression/medication and reversible contributors, identify the likely syndrome, assess safety/capacity functionally, and centre autonomy, quality of life and caregiver support.
recognize: Memory, executive, language, visuospatial or behavioural decline can predominate depending on etiology.
Loss of IADLs often precedes basic ADL dependence.
differentiate: Delirium is acute/fluctuating inattention and should not be diagnosed as dementia progression.
Depression, sleep/sensory problems, medications and metabolic disease can worsen cognition.
assessment: Obtain patient and collateral history, cognition, ADLs/IADLs, mood, medications, hearing/vision, driving, wandering, falls, finances, caregiver strain and neurologic findings.
workup: Use validated cognitive testing and targeted labs; neuroimaging is selected for atypical/rapid/focal/young presentations or when it will change diagnosis.
management: Address vascular and reversible factors, use cognition-symptom medications when appropriate, support routines/safety and caregiver/community resources, and plan advance care while capacity allows.
medicationSafety: Avoid anticholinergic burden and routine antipsychotics for behavioural symptoms without dangerous distress after non-drug causes/interventions are addressed.
counselling: Use person-first, non-stigmatizing language and support participation in decisions for as long as possible.
followUp: Track function, safety, caregiver needs and medication benefit/adverse effects.
examTrap: Diagnosing dementia during an acute UTI-associated delirium or from a screening score without functional decline.
oneLinePearl: Dementia is chronic cognitive decline plus functional impact; delirium is acute brain failure.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada Dementia Strategy and 2025 annual report

title: Delirium Prevention and Management: Acute Brain Failure Has a Cause
bottomLine: Acute fluctuating inattention and cognitive change is delirium until a precipitating cause is found. Treat causes and restore orientation, mobility, sleep, hydration, pain control and sensory input; sedatives/antipsychotics do not cure delirium and may worsen harm.
recognize: Hypoactive delirium is common and easily missed.
Infection, hypoxia, medications, withdrawal, pain, retention, constipation, dehydration and metabolic disease are common precipitants.
differentiate: Dementia is chronic/progressive; delirium changes over hours to days and impairs attention.
A positive urine test alone does not prove UTI as the cause of delirium.
assessment: Establish baseline cognition/function from collateral, assess attention/fluctuation, vitals/oxygenation/glucose, pain, medications, withdrawal, retention/constipation, hydration and neurologic findings.
workup: Use cause-directed labs/imaging/urinalysis rather than a universal delirium panel; image for trauma/focal/other neurologic concerns.
management: Correct causes, mobilize, orient, optimize hearing/vision, normalize sleep and reduce unnecessary lines/restraints.
Use medication only for severe dangerous agitation when non-drug measures fail and after reviewing contraindications.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines worsen most delirium except specific withdrawal indications; anticholinergics/sedatives are common contributors.
counselling: Explain to family that recovery can lag after the trigger is treated.
followUp: Reassess cognition after recovery because delirium can unmask underlying impairment.
examTrap: Treating bacteriuria with antibiotics solely because an older adult is delirious without urinary/systemic evidence of infection.
oneLinePearl: Delirium is a symptom of acute illness; find the trigger before sedating the behaviour.

title: Depression in Older Adults: Function, Suicide Risk, Cognition, and Medical Mimics
bottomLine: Late-life depression may present with somatic complaints, cognitive concern, withdrawal or functional decline. Diagnose the syndrome, assess suicide risk and bipolarity, review grief/medical/medication contributors, and treat while minimizing falls, hyponatremia, anticholinergic and interaction burden.
recognize: Anhedonia and functional withdrawal may be more obvious than stated sadness.
Depression and dementia can coexist; improvement with mood treatment does not exclude underlying cognitive disease.
differentiate: Delirium is acute/fluctuating; bereavement does not exclude major depression when syndrome/impairment criteria are met.
Hypothyroidism, anemia, sleep disorders, pain and medications can contribute.
assessment: Assess symptoms/function, suicide/self-neglect, mania history, alcohol/substances, grief/isolation, cognition, medications, pain and supports.
workup: Use validated scales for severity and targeted medical tests when contributors are plausible.
management: Use psychotherapy, social activation and pharmacotherapy according to severity/preference; urgent care for suicidal, psychotic, catatonic or severe self-neglect presentations.
medicationSafety: Monitor sodium, falls, bleeding/interactions and anticholinergic burden according to agent/risk; start/titrate thoughtfully without undertreating severe illness.
counselling: Avoid attributing depression to 'just getting old' and address social isolation/access.
followUp: Track mood, function, adverse effects and cognition after treatment changes.
examTrap: Starting an anticholinergic TCA for insomnia/depression in a frail fall-prone adult without considering safer options.
oneLinePearl: Late-life depression is treatable illness, not normal aging.
sourceBasis: Canadian geriatric psychiatry and depression practice resources

title: Anxiety in Older Adults: Treat the Pattern Without Creating Sedative Harm
bottomLine: New or worsening anxiety in older adults requires assessment for medical illness, medication/substance effects, depression, cognitive disease and social stressors. Prefer psychotherapy and appropriate maintenance treatment over chronic benzodiazepine rescue that increases falls, cognitive impairment and dependence.
recognize: Anxiety can present as somatic symptoms, repeated reassurance seeking, sleep disturbance or avoidance.
Late-life new-onset anxiety can be secondary to illness or medication and deserves a medical differential.
differentiate: Delirium, arrhythmia, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycemia, dyspnea and withdrawal can mimic panic/anxiety.
Akathisia or medication side effects may be described as anxiety.
assessment: Assess onset, triggers, avoidance/function, depression/suicide, cognition, sleep, substances, medications, cardiopulmonary/endocrine symptoms and isolation/caregiver stress.
workup: Use targeted testing for medical mimics rather than broad panels once a stable psychiatric pattern is established.
management: Use CBT/behavioural approaches, social supports and evidence-based maintenance pharmacotherapy when needed; taper chronic benzodiazepines gradually when risks exceed benefits.
medicationSafety: Avoid combining benzodiazepines with opioids/alcohol and avoid abrupt withdrawal after dependence.
counselling: Explain that reducing sedatives can improve balance and cognition while anxiety is treated by other means.
followUp: Track function, falls, sleep and medication burden as well as anxiety symptoms.
examTrap: Prescribing nightly benzodiazepines indefinitely for new anxiety without reviewing falls, cognition and medical causes.
oneLinePearl: In older adults, anxiety treatment should reduce distress without adding fall and cognitive risk.

title: Urinary Incontinence in Older Adults: Identify the Type and Reversible Contributors
bottomLine: Incontinence is not an inevitable consequence of aging. Distinguish urgency, stress, overflow and functional incontinence, assess reversible contributors and mobility/environment, then use bladder training, pelvic-floor/functional interventions and selective medication rather than reflex anticholinergic prescribing.
recognize: Urgency/frequency suggests overactive bladder; leakage with cough/exertion suggests stress; high residual/weak stream suggests overflow.
Functional incontinence reflects inability to reach/use the toilet because of mobility, cognition or environment.
differentiate: UTI requires compatible symptoms; bacteriuria alone does not explain chronic incontinence.
New incontinence can be driven by delirium, stool impaction, diuretics, hyperglycemia or mobility change.
assessment: Review pattern/diary, fluid/caffeine, bowel function, medications, mobility/cognition, pelvic/prostate history, neurologic signs and red flags.
workup: Use urinalysis only when infection/hematuria question exists and postvoid residual when retention/overflow is suspected; avoid routine urodynamics for uncomplicated initial care.
management: Treat reversible causes, use scheduled toileting/bladder training/pelvic-floor therapy and improve access/mobility.
Use drugs selectively after cognitive/fall/constipation burden review and refer retention/hematuria/prolapse/complex disease.
medicationSafety: Antimuscarinics can worsen cognition, constipation and retention; review total anticholinergic burden.
counselling: Normalize discussion without normalizing the symptom as inevitable aging.
followUp: Track episodes, function and adverse effects rather than continuing ineffective therapy.
examTrap: Adding an anticholinergic to a delirious constipated older adult with new incontinence without checking retention and medications.
oneLinePearl: Treat the incontinence type and the reversible contributors before adding bladder medication.

title: Constipation in Older Adults: Medications, Mobility, Intake, and Alarm Features
bottomLine: Constipation in older adults is commonly multifactorial. Review medications, mobility, hydration/nutrition, toileting access and pelvic/neurologic disease; look for impaction and alarm features before escalating laxatives or ordering routine colonoscopy.
recognize: Opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium and reduced mobility commonly contribute.
Overflow diarrhea can occur around fecal impaction.
differentiate: New constipation with weight loss, bleeding, anemia or obstruction symptoms is not routine functional constipation.
Medication-related and slow-transit/outlet disorders require different solutions.
assessment: Review baseline/tempo, stool form/frequency, straining, incomplete evacuation, pain, bleeding, weight, diet/fluid, mobility, cognition, toileting, medications and rectal/neurologic features.
workup: Use targeted labs/imaging/endoscopy only when secondary cause/alarm feature is present; assess for impaction when suggested clinically.
management: Address causative medications and mobility/intake, use appropriate osmotic/stimulant regimens and scheduled bowel plans for high-risk patients.
Opioid therapy should include proactive bowel management when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic magnesium/phosphate products in significant renal impairment unless specifically appropriate; monitor dehydration/electrolytes with aggressive regimens.
counselling: Set realistic bowel goals and reduce stigma.
followUp: Reassess efficacy and need for further structural/outlet evaluation.
examTrap: Treating overflow diarrhea with antidiarrheals in a patient with fecal impaction.
oneLinePearl: Constipation care begins with cause and impaction—not a stronger laxative by default.

title: Nutrition and Unintentional Weight Loss in Older Adults: Find the Cause Before Supplements
bottomLine: Unintentional weight loss in an older adult is a clinical signal, not normal aging. Confirm trajectory and intake, then assess oral/dental/swallowing disease, depression/dementia, medications, social access, malignancy, inflammatory disease and other medical causes before relying on supplements alone.
recognize: Loss of weight, muscle, appetite or function can accelerate frailty and falls.
Food insecurity, isolation and inability to shop/cook are medical-plan determinants.
differentiate: Intentional weight change differs from unexplained loss; edema can mask true tissue loss.
Cachexia, malnutrition and sarcopenia overlap but are not interchangeable.
assessment: Quantify weight trajectory, intake, swallowing/dental issues, GI symptoms, mood/cognition, medications, functional ability, finances/food access and systemic symptoms.
workup: Use targeted CBC/chemistry/thyroid/inflammatory or cancer evaluation based on phenotype; swallowing assessment when aspiration/dysphagia is suspected.
management: Treat cause, optimize protein/energy intake, feeding assistance/oral health and social supports; use dietitian/SLP/geriatric resources where indicated.
Avoid overly restrictive diets when benefits are small and intake/function suffer.
medicationSafety: Review anorexia/nausea-inducing medications and avoid appetite stimulants with poor benefit-risk unless a specific indication exists.
counselling: Prioritize enjoyable adequate intake and function rather than moralizing weight.
followUp: Track weight, intake, strength/function and diagnostic closure.
examTrap: Prescribing a supplement while ignoring new dysphagia and 10% unintentional weight loss.
oneLinePearl: Unintentional weight loss is a diagnosis to explain, not a normal-aging finding.

title: Sleep Disorders in Older Adults: Diagnose the Driver Before Sedating
bottomLine: Sleep changes with aging, but chronic insomnia, apnea, restless legs, circadian disruption, pain, mood disease and medications require distinct management. CBT-I and treatment of the underlying sleep disorder are preferred over chronic benzodiazepine/Z-drug sedation that raises falls and cognitive risk.
recognize: OSA causes snoring/apneas/daytime sleepiness; insomnia causes difficulty sleeping despite opportunity and distress/impairment.
Nocturia, pain, depression/anxiety and medications can fragment sleep.
differentiate: Reduced sleep need with activation may be mania; sleepiness is not the same as fatigue.
Delirium-related reversal of sleep-wake cycle is an acute illness signal.
assessment: Review schedule, naps, caffeine/alcohol, snoring/apneas, restless legs, pain/nocturia, mood, medications and daytime function/falls.
workup: Use sleep study for suspected sleep-disordered breathing/selected disorders, not routine uncomplicated insomnia.
management: Use CBT-I/stimulus control/sleep consolidation and treat OSA/restless legs/pain/mood contributors.
Deprescribe chronic sedative-hypnotics gradually when risk exceeds benefit.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines/Z-drugs increase falls, cognitive impairment and dependence and interact dangerously with opioids/alcohol.
counselling: Explain that sleep efficiency and daytime function matter more than an arbitrary 8-hour target.
followUp: Track sleep/function and sedative taper response.
examTrap: Starting nightly benzodiazepine for insomnia before asking about OSA, falls and alcohol use.
oneLinePearl: Treat the sleep disorder, not the clock, and avoid buying sleep with falls.

title: Chronic Pain in Older Adults: Function, Multimodal Treatment, and Medication Burden
bottomLine: Chronic pain care in older adults targets function, sleep and participation while identifying treatable causes. Use multimodal non-drug and cause-specific therapy and select medications with renal/hepatic, falls, cognition, constipation and interaction risks in mind; opioids require explicit goals and monitoring rather than reflex avoidance or escalation.
recognize: Pain may present as reduced mobility, appetite, mood or sleep rather than a high numeric score.
Neuropathic, nociceptive and centralized pain respond to different treatments.
differentiate: New focal/night pain, fracture, infection, malignancy or inflammatory disease is not routine chronic pain.
Behaviour change in dementia can signal pain but has many other causes.
assessment: Assess pain mechanism, function/goals, mood/sleep, falls, cognition, substance history, renal/hepatic function and current analgesic/sedative burden.
workup: Use cause-directed imaging/labs only when findings would change management; avoid repeated imaging for stable nonspecific pain without red flags.
management: Use exercise/PT/OT, pacing, psychological and local/non-opioid options where appropriate, then individualized pharmacotherapy.
If opioids are used, define functional benefit, dose review, constipation/sedation safety and taper when harms exceed benefit.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs can worsen GI/renal/CV risk; gabapentinoids, opioids and sedatives increase falls/respiratory depression, especially in combination.
counselling: Set functional goals and explain that complete pain elimination is often unrealistic and can drive harmful escalation.
followUp: Continue therapy only when benefit outweighs harm and reassess function, falls, cognition and bowel effects.
examTrap: Escalating an opioid because the pain score is unchanged while walking, alertness and falls worsen.
oneLinePearl: Older-adult pain treatment succeeds when function improves without trading it for sedation and falls.
